questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks’ gestation is admitted to the hospital 60 minutes after awakening with painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 118/84 mm Hg. The uterus is soft and nontender. The fundal height is 34 cm. The fetus is in an oblique lie with the head in the left lower quadrant. External fetal monitoring shows no contractions. The fetal heart rate is 156/min with no decelerations and normal variability. There is minimal flow of bright red blood at the introitus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Intravenous administration of fluids and observation

correctExplanation: Placenta previa refers to the abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. It most commonly presents with painless third trimester vaginal bleeding. Frequently, it is detected on prenatal ultrasonography, but it may not always be evident. Thus, patients who present with vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks’ gestation should not undergo a digital cervical examination until ultrasonography has been performed to determine the exact positioning of the placenta because severe hemorrhage can occur if a placenta previa is present. Risk factors for placenta previa include causes of uterine scarring, such as multiparity, previous cesarean delivery, and prior dilatation and curettage. While it may self-resolve as pregnancy progresses, its presence in the late third trimester requires careful management. Treatment of an initial bleed without significant hemodynamic instability, such as in this patient, necessitates intravenous administration of fluids and observation. Patients who are able to be stabilized may be expectantly managed with a plan for a cesarean delivery around 37 weeks’ gestation, to allow time for sufficient fetal development. A cesarean delivery is indicated to prevent significant hemorrhage, maternal/fetal complications, and potential fetal demise. Immediate cesarean delivery is advised for patients who present in labor or those with hemodynamically significant bleeding. questionStem: An otherwise asymptomatic 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of irregular vaginal bleeding since she underwent tubal ligation 2 years ago. Prior to tubal ligation, she used an oral contraceptive for 10 years. Since tubal ligation, menses have been occurring at 21- to 56-day intervals and lasting 5 to 13 days. All three of her deliveries we 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 90 kg (198 Ib); BMI is 32 kg/m2. Physical examin ion shows no abnormalities. An abnormality of which of the following serum concentrations is most consistent with the suspected diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, and hirsutism, often in patients with an increased body weight. It requires two of the following for diagnosis: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism. It is associated with signs of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans and increased blood glucose concentrations. PCOS is associated with an abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback response, which leads to increased luteinizing hormone (LH) in comparison to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), as well as markedly increased androgen production from the theca lutein cells. This results in an increased serum concentration of testosterone. Treatment includes weight loss, oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, and spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism. Clomiphene stimulates ovulation and can also be used for patients desiring pregnancy. If the patient is diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, oral medications (eg, metformin) or insulin may also be necessary. A potential complication of long-standing PCOS is endometrial cancer due to the chronic anovulation resulting in prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen.

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 32-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 1 hour after awakening with vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping. She has not had her first prenatal visit. Her pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 127/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows mild bleeding from a closed cervical os. The uterus is consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Endovaginal ultrasonography shows a gestational sac with an 8-week fetal pole and visible fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Determination of blood type and Rh factor

correctExplanation: Rh(D)-negative mothers are at a high risk for developing anti-D antibodies if exposed to blood from an Rh(D)-positive fetus, which most commonly occurs during delivery. However, it can also occur during episodes of fetomaternal bleeding during pregnancy, such as that seen in this patient, likely secondary to a threatened abortion (eg, vaginal bleeding with a closed os prior to 20 weeks’ gestation). If Rnh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother’s immune system will form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen. This can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (eg, erythroblastosis fetalis) if the fetus is Rh(D)- positive, as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when they cross the placenta. Rh,(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh(D)-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh(D) antigen. Administration of Rh,(D) immune globulin is typically performed for Rh(D)-negative mothers at 28 weeks’ gestation, along with following the delivery of an Rh(D)-positive newborn, any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to determine this patient's blood type and Rh factor, so she may be given Rh,(D) immune globulin if necessary.

Anovulation can be caused by pregnancy, polycystic ovary syndrome, abnormalities or immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, menopause or premature ovarian failure, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. questionStem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks’ gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor 2 hours after the onset of contractions and spontaneous rupture of membranes. Contractions occur every 2 minutes and last 45 seconds. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The cervix is 5 cm dilated and 100% effaced; the vertex is at —2 station. A fetal heart tracing is shown. Labor progresses during the next 3 hours. At delivery, the newborn is limp and pale. Apgar scores are 3 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A healthy fetal heart rate is between 110 and 160 beats per minute (bpm) with 6 to 25 bpm of variability and spontaneous accelerations. Intermittent early and variable decelerations can also occur during the normal process of labor as a result of head compression and umbilical cord compression, respectively. In comparison, uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia can present with late decelerations on the fetal heart rate tracing, which are defined as gradual decreases in the fetal heart rate that begin after the peak of uterine contraction and nadir more than 30 seconds after the initiation of heart rate decline. Risk factors for the development of uteroplacental insufficiency are hypertension, diabetes, anemia, cocaine or tobacco use, coagulopathies, late-term pregnancy, and uterine infection. Fetal hypoxemia can also be caused by severe uterine contractions and maternal hypotension or hypoxia. Treatment consists of supplemental oxygenation, movement of the patient onto her left side or onto all fours, and intravenous fluids. If late decelerations persist on fetal heart rate tracings, then an urgent cesarean delivery is indicated, as continued uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia will result in deleterious effects on the fetus. This patient progressed through labor having consistent late decelerations, indicating that the fetus was probably experiencing recurrent fetal hypoxemia and consequent fetal metabolic acidemia, which are likely responsible for this newborn’s presentation on delivery.

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of vulvar itching and discomfort despite treatment with over-the- counter antifungal creams. She is sexually active with one male partner. Physical examination shows several 1-cm, small, firm left inguinal lymph nodes. Pelvic examination shows mild edema and excoriations over the labia majora and minora. There is a 1-cm, tender, raised lesion with an ulcerated center and erythematous edges at the base of the left labium majus. The cervix, vaginal mucosa, uterus, and adnexa are normal. There is a white discharge with no odor in the vaginal canal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vulvar carcinoma most commonly presents in older patients with a lesion on the labia majora that is often asymptomatic. The lesion may be a nodule, papule, or plaque, with varying degrees of ulceration. When present, other symptoms include pruritus or bleeding from the lesion. In addition to the lesion, physical examination may show inguinal lymphadenopathy, as seen in this patient, if the vulvar cancer has metastasized. The most frequent underlying histopathology is squamous cell carcinoma, and incidence is greatest in patients between the age 55 and 85 years. Risk factors include infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), cigarette smoking, immunosuppression, chronic inflammation (eg, lichen sclerosus), and a history of cervical cancer. Diagnosis is made with a biopsy of the lesion. Further evaluation should include cervical cancer screening, as concurrent cervical carcinoma is common, and abdominopelvic imaging to determine extent of disease. Treatment includes surgical excision and chemoradiation.

The head circumference is below the 5th percentile for gestational age. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 40/min. Funduscopic examination shows chorioretinitis. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Serum studies show AST activity of 247 U/L and ALT activity of 196 U/L. ACT scan of the head shows scattered intracerebral calcifications. Which of the following intrauterine organisms is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is asymptomatic at birth in approximately 90% of newborns. When symptomatic in utero, ultrasonography may show hepatosplenomegaly, intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, or intracerebral (most often periventricular) calcifications. Fetal hydrops is a potential complication. Clinical features in symptomatic newborns include the above as well as transaminitis, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, petechiae, chorioretinitis, small size for gestational age, seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss. Long-term sequela in symptomatic infants, such as sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental abnormalities, are common. The risk for symptomatic neonatal infection is higher with a primary maternal infection than with recurrent infection. In adults, CMV is often asymptomatic or can cause a short, febrile, flu-like illness. Congenital CMV is the most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss and can present later in childhood in up to 10% of children who were asymptomatic at birth. Diagnosis of neonatal CMV can be confirmed with polymerase chain reaction testing or culture of urine or saliva. Treatment involves 6 months of oral valganciclovir and close, interdisciplinary follow-up.
